lesson.title: Classful Addressing: The Original, Now Obsolete, Way IPv4 Carved Up Its Address Space
lesson.summary: The IPv4 address class system encoded a default network size directly into an address's leading bits, splitting the space into classes A through E before CIDR replaced fixed class boundaries with flexible subnet masks.
lesson.body:
Before routers could easily be told an arbitrary network size, early IPv4 needed some way to answer a basic question just by looking at an address: how many of its bits belong to the network, and how many belong to the host within that network. The address class system, defined in RFC 791 alongside IPv4 itself, answered that question by encoding the split directly into the leading bits of the first octet, so a router could tell a network's default size from the address alone without any extra configuration.

Class A addresses have a leading bit of 0, which restricts the first octet to values 0 through 127, though 0 is reserved and the entire 127.0.0.0 through 127.255.255.255 block is reserved for loopback addresses, leaving the usable Class A range as 1.0.0.0 through 126.255.255.255. Class A used a default mask of 255.0.0.0, an 8 bit network portion, leaving 24 bits, roughly 16.7 million addresses per network, for hosts, which is why Class A blocks were handed out almost exclusively to the largest early networks and government agencies.

Class B addresses have leading bits 10, restricting the first octet to 128 through 191, and used a default mask of 255.255.0.0, a 16 bit network portion and a 16 bit host portion, giving roughly 65,534 usable host addresses per network. Class C addresses have leading bits 110, restricting the first octet to 192 through 223, and used a default mask of 255.255.255.0, a 24 bit network portion and only an 8 bit host portion, giving just 254 usable host addresses, which made Class C the right fit for smaller organizations but meant medium sized ones often had to be handed several Class C blocks or one oversized Class B block, wasting huge numbers of addresses either way.

Two further classes exist outside the normal unicast addressing scheme. Class D addresses have leading bits 1110, spanning 224.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255, and are reserved for multicast, where a single packet is delivered to a group of interested receivers rather than one destination. Class E addresses have leading bits 1111, spanning 240.0.0.0 through 255.255.255.255, and were set aside for experimental use, largely unused in ordinary networking.

The rigid A, B, C boundaries wasted address space badly, since an organization needing 300 host addresses had no efficient option between a Class C block with only 254 and a Class B block with 65,534, which is exactly the pressure that led to Classless Inter Domain Routing (CIDR) replacing address classes with arbitrary length subnet masks in the early 1990s. Modern IPv4 addressing is classless in practice, but the old class boundaries still explain historically why certain ranges, like the entire 127.0.0.0/8 loopback block or the private ranges defined in RFC 1918, land where they do within the IPv4 address format.
